problems.fix: Nothing shows for weeks and people often dig the row over by mistake. Soak the seed overnight before sowing. Keep the soil moist and give it up to six weeks.

parsley.source: Parsley care: RHS. pH: Cornell and University of Maryland extension.

coriander.about: Coriander leaves (cilantro) are ready fast and the seeds come later. In heat or dry soil the plants soon shoot up and flower. So sow a small batch every month or so from spring, rather than one big sowing. It grows well in a pot.
coriander.water: It needs a normal amount of water. In dry spells keep the soil moist, because dry roots make it flower early. In warm weather, check pots every day.
coriander.feed: Coriander needs very little. It's a quick crop, so garden soil or fresh compost is enough without any feed.
coriander.harvest: Start cutting leaves when the plants are 10 to 15 cm tall. Take a few from each plant, then give them about two weeks to grow back. For seed, let some plants flower. Cut the stems when the seeds turn brown and dry them in a paper bag.
coriander.keeps: A fresh bunch lasts a few days in the fridge. Dried seed keeps for months in an airtight jar.

problems.name: Bolting
problems.fix: In hot, dry weather or after being moved, the plants send up a flower stalk and stop making leaves. Sow the seed where the plants will grow, in a spot with shade at midday. Water in dry spells and choose a variety that is slow to bolt.

problems.name: Slugs and snails
problems.fix: In damp weather they eat the seedlings. Go out after dark and pick them off.

problems.name: Aphids
problems.fix: Small green or black insects crowd onto the shoot tips and weaken the plant. Rub them off or wash them away. Leave ladybirds alone, as they eat them.

coriander.source: Coriander care: RHS. pH: University of Connecticut extension. Pot size: Oregon State extension.

dill.about: Dill gives you feathery leaves and, later on, seeds. It has one long main root and hates being moved. So sow it where it will grow, a little at a time every few weeks from mid-spring to midsummer. Like coriander, it bolts in hot, dry weather, which means it flowers too soon.
dill.water: Normal watering suits dill. Water it in dry spells, because dry soil makes it flower early and stop making leaves. Pots dry out quickly in warm weather.
dill.feed: It needs little food. In garden soil or fresh compost, you don't need to feed it at all.
dill.harvest: You can start picking leaves about six weeks after sowing. Take a few at a time and leave at least a third of the plant. For seed, cut the heads in late summer when they are dry and brown. Hang them upside down in a paper bag.
dill.keeps: Fresh leaves wilt fast and don't keep well, even in the fridge. Use them soon or dry them. Dried leaves and seeds keep in an airtight jar.

problems.name: Bolting
problems.fix: In hot, dry weather the plants flower early and stop making leaves. Water in dry spells and sow again every few weeks. If you only want leaves, cut off the flower stems.

problems.name: Aphids
problems.fix: Small green or black insects cluster on the soft shoots and leaves. Rub or wash them off. Leave the ladybirds alone to eat the ones you miss.

problems.name: Slugs and snails
problems.fix: In damp weather they eat the tender seedlings. Check after dark and pick them off.

dill.source: Dill care: RHS. pH: University of Connecticut extension.

chervil.about: This small, delicate herb has a mild taste of aniseed. It likes cool weather and light shade. In hot sun it flowers too soon, so it does best in spring and autumn. Sow a little every few weeks for a steady supply.
chervil.water: Chervil needs normal watering. Keep the soil evenly damp but not soggy, as dry soil makes it flower early. Pots need extra water in warm weather.
chervil.feed: It needs very little food. Garden soil or fresh compost is enough, so don't feed it.
chervil.harvest: The leaves are ready about eight weeks after sowing, once the plants are 10 cm tall. Pick a few young leaves from each plant. Or cut whole stems back to 5 cm and let them grow again.
chervil.keeps: Use chervil fresh. It wilts within a day or two and it loses most of its flavour when dried.

problems.name: Bolting
problems.fix: In hot sun and dry soil the plants flower early and the leaves lose their taste. Grow it in light shade, water regularly and sow again every few weeks.

problems.name: Aphids
problems.fix: Small green insects cluster on the soft leaves and shoots. Rub or wash them off and let ladybirds eat the rest.

chervil.source: Chervil care: RHS. pH: University of Connecticut extension.

chives.about: The leaves taste mildly of onion and you can eat the purple flowers too. The clump comes back every spring. Every three or four years, dig it up, pull it into smaller clumps and replant them to keep it strong.
chives.water: Chives need normal watering. In the first summer, water them in dry spells. After that, chives in the ground manage on their own. In a pot, keep the compost evenly moist.
chives.feed: They need little food. In the ground, some compost at planting time is enough. In a pot, a general liquid feed now and then in summer keeps new leaves coming.
chives.harvest: Snip leaves just above the base whenever you need them. The more often you cut, the more you get. After flowering, cut the whole clump back to about 5 cm and it will send up lots of fresh leaves.
chives.keeps: Cut chives wilt within a few days. To use them in winter, chop them and freeze them in a bag or an ice cube tray.

problems.name: Rust
problems.fix: Raised orange spots appear on the leaves. Cut the clump right back and put the leaves in the bin. The new growth usually comes up clean.

problems.name: Aphids
problems.fix: Small greenfly cluster on the leaves and flower stalks. Rub them off or wash them off with a jet of water.

chives.source: Chive care: RHS. pH: University of Minnesota extension.

thyme.about: Thyme stays green all year, so you can pick it fresh in any season or dry it. It's a small shrub that needs sun and soil where water drains away fast. Wet ground in winter kills it more often than cold does. After a few years the plants turn woody. Replace them with new plants grown from cuttings.
thyme.water: Thyme copes well with dry spells. Water new plants in dry weather until they settle in. After that, plants in the ground rarely need water. In a pot, water in hot, dry weather and let the compost dry out a little in between.
thyme.feed: It needs very little food. Thyme grows best in poor soil, so don't feed it in the ground. Rich soil gives soft growth with less flavour. A plant that has been in the same pot for over a year can have a light sprinkle of general fertiliser in late spring.
thyme.harvest: Snip sprigs whenever you need them. The soft new growth of late spring and summer has the best flavour. Cutting it often keeps the plant compact. Trim it lightly after flowering, but don't cut into the bare wood.
thyme.keeps: Fresh sprigs keep a few days in a bag in the fridge. To dry thyme, hang bunches in a warm, dark, airy place for a few weeks. Then keep the leaves in an airtight jar.

problems.name: Root rot
problems.fix: The plant wilts and turns brown from the base while the soil is wet. Grow it in soil that drains fast, a raised bed or a pot with grit mixed in. Never leave a pot standing in water.

problems.name: Bare, woody plant
problems.fix: After a few years the middle of the plant goes bare and woody. Trim it lightly every year after flowering. Replace old plants with cuttings taken in late spring.

problems.name: Rosemary beetle
problems.fix: Small beetles with metallic green and purple stripes eat the leaves from late summer to spring. Their grey grubs eat them too. Pick them off by hand or shake the plant over a sheet of paper.

thyme.source: Thyme care: RHS. pH: University of Connecticut soil testing lab.

rosemary.about: You can pick rosemary all year, as this shrub keeps its leaves in every season. Give it full sun and soil that drains quickly. Wet, heavy ground kills it faster than cold does. In cold areas, grow it against a sunny wall or in a pot you can move to shelter.
rosemary.water: Rosemary handles dry spells well. In the first year, water it when the weather is dry. After that, plants in the ground rarely need water. A pot needs water in hot weather, but never let the compost get waterlogged.
rosemary.feed: It needs very little food. Plants in the ground don't need feeding at all. If a plant has been in the same pot for more than a year, give it some general fertiliser granules in late spring or early summer.
rosemary.harvest: Snip shoots whenever you need them, all year round. The soft new growth of late spring and summer tastes best. Trim the plant after flowering to keep it bushy. Don't cut into old, bare wood, because it rarely sprouts again.
rosemary.keeps: Fresh sprigs keep several days in the fridge. To dry them, hang them in a warm, dark, airy place. Then strip off the leaves and keep them in an airtight jar.

problems.name: Rosemary beetle
problems.fix: From late summer to spring, small beetles with metallic green and purple stripes eat the leaves and so do their grey grubs. Pick them off by hand or shake the plant over a sheet of paper.

problems.name: Frost and wet damage
problems.fix: Shoots turn brown and die after a hard frost, cold wind or a wet winter. In very cold spells, cover the plant with fleece and move pots somewhere sheltered. Cut out the dead shoots in spring.

problems.name: Cuckoo spit
problems.fix: Blobs of white froth appear on the shoots in late spring. Each one hides a small insect that sucks sap. It does little harm, so wipe it off or rinse it away with water.

rosemary.source: Rosemary care: RHS. pH: Texas A&M AgriLife extension.

oregano.about: You can use oregano fresh or dried. It spreads out over time and comes back every year. Most of the top dies back in winter and new shoots come up in spring. It has the most flavour in full sun and in poor soil that drains quickly. It's best picked just before the flowers open.
oregano.water: Once settled, oregano copes with dry spells. Water new plants when it's dry. Settled plants in the ground need no extra water. In a pot, water it in hot, dry weather, but never let the compost stay soggy.
oregano.feed: Oregano needs very little food. Plants in the ground need no feeding. A plant that has been in the same pot for more than a year can have a sprinkle of general fertiliser granules in late spring or early summer.
oregano.harvest: Pick shoots from late spring to autumn and strip off the leaves. The flavour is best before the flowers open. After flowering, cut the plant back and it will grow a fresh batch of leaves. Clear away the old stems in late winter.
oregano.keeps: It dries well. Hang sprigs in a dark, airy place for a few weeks. Then strip off the leaves and keep them in an airtight jar.

problems.name: Mint rust
problems.fix: Orange or brown powdery spots appear under the leaves and shoots come up twisted in spring. Cut the affected stems down to the ground. Put them in the bin, not on the compost.

problems.name: Leafhoppers
problems.fix: Small jumping insects suck the sap and leave pale, blotchy patches on the leaves. The damage only spoils the look, so you can leave them alone.

problems.name: Mint moth
problems.fix: Small caterpillars eat the leaves in summer and spin them together. The damage is usually slight. Pick off the caterpillars if it bothers you.

oregano.source: Oregano care: RHS. pH: University of Connecticut soil testing lab (marjoram) and NC State extension.

sage.about: Soft grey-green leaves stay on this shrub all year, so you can pick sage in any season. It needs sun and soil that never stays soggy. After six or seven years the plants get woody and straggly. Then replace them with new plants grown from cuttings.
sage.water: Sage copes with dry spells once it has settled. Water it in dry weather during the first year. After that, plants in the ground can take drought. In a pot, keep the compost just moist, not soggy. In winter, move the pot beside a wall, out of the rain.
sage.feed: It needs very little food. Don't feed plants in the ground at all. If a plant has been in the same pot for more than a year, give it a light sprinkle of general fertiliser granules in late spring or early summer.
sage.harvest: Pick young leaves or whole shoots whenever you need them. Growth from spring and summer tastes best. Picking often keeps the plant bushy. Give it a light trim every year in mid to late spring.
sage.keeps: To dry sage, hang sprigs in a warm, dark, airy place. Then keep the leaves in an airtight jar. You can also chop the leaves and freeze them in an ice cube tray.

problems.name: Rosemary beetle
problems.fix: Small beetles striped in metallic green and purple eat the leaves from late summer to spring. Their grey grubs do the same. Pick them off by hand or shake the plant over a sheet of paper.

problems.name: Leafhoppers
problems.fix: Pale, blotchy patches on the leaves come from small jumping insects that suck sap. The damage is rarely serious. Just pick off the worst leaves.

problems.name: Woody, straggly plant
problems.fix: Old plants grow long, bare stems with few leaves. Trim lightly every spring. Every few years, take cuttings from the soft new shoots in late spring to replace the plant.

sage.source: Sage care: RHS. pH: UC Master Gardeners, University of California.

mint.about: This fast grower lasts for years and goes into tea, drinks and cooking. Its roots run fast underground and take over a bed. So grow it in a pot, or sink a pot with no bottom into the ground with the rim above the soil. It dies down in winter and comes back in spring.
mint.water: Mint needs a lot of water. Keep the soil evenly moist, because it wilts fast in a dry pot. Check pots often in summer and move them into light shade when it's hot.
mint.feed: Mint needs average feeding, mostly in pots. In the ground it needs little. Give a potted plant liquid fertiliser in spring, then every 4 to 6 weeks while it grows.
mint.harvest: From late spring to autumn, pick the young shoot tips often. Regular picking keeps the plant compact and full of fresh growth. Cut back stems that are flowering to get new leaves.
mint.keeps: Fresh sprigs keep a few days in a glass of water or in the fridge. Freezing keeps the flavour better than drying. Freeze the leaves in ice cubes.

problems.name: Mint rust
problems.fix: Orange powdery spots appear under the leaves and in spring the shoots come up twisted and swollen. Cut affected stems to the ground and put them in the bin. If it comes back every year, start again with healthy plants in a new spot.

problems.name: Spreading everywhere
problems.fix: Creeping shoots pop up all over the bed. Keep mint in a pot with the rim above the soil, so the runners can't climb over it. Every few years, split the plant into pieces and repot it.

problems.name: Mint beetle
problems.fix: In summer, small shiny blue-green beetles and their grubs eat holes in the leaves. Pick them off. The plant usually grows back.

mint.source: Mint care: RHS. pH: NSW Department of Primary Industries. Feeding in pots: University of Arizona extension.

tulip.about: Big, bright tulips flower in mid to late spring. Plant the bulbs late in autumn, in soil that drains well and doesn't stay wet. Bulbs planted late get tulip fire, a fungal disease, less often. Many tulips only flower well in their first year. Where it matters most, plant fresh bulbs every year.
tulip.water: Tulips need normal watering. Once the shoots are up, bulbs in the ground only need water after two or three weeks without rain. Keep pots watered from when the leaves appear, as drought cuts the flowering short. If the compost in a pot stays sodden in winter, move it out of the rain.
tulip.feed: An average amount of feeding suits them. From early spring, give tulips in pots a high-potassium liquid feed, such as tomato feed, every week until the leaves turn yellow.
tulip.harvest: For the vase, cut them when the bud shows colour but hasn't opened yet. In the garden, cut off faded flowers just above the leaves. Leave the leaves until they turn the colour of straw. To keep the bulbs, dig them up about six weeks after flowering. Dry them and store them somewhere warm, dark and airy until autumn.
tulip.keeps: Cut tulips last several days in a vase. They keep growing and bend towards the light. Top up the vase with cold water.

problems.name: Tulip fire
problems.fix: Brown spots appear and the leaves and flowers twist and wither, sometimes with grey mould. Dig out sick plants with their bulbs and put them in the bin. Plant late in autumn and grow tulips somewhere else for at least three years.

problems.name: Squirrels and mice
problems.fix: They dig up the bulbs and eat them in autumn and winter. Cover the bed or pot with chicken wire until the leaves are up. Daffodils planted among them help, as squirrels avoid them.

problems.name: Few or no flowers
problems.fix: From the second year on you get leaves but no flowers, or only small ones. Plant bulbs at least three times their own height deep and feed pots while the leaves are up. Replace tired bulbs with fresh ones.

tulip.source: Tulip care: RHS. pH: University of Connecticut soil testing lab. Pot size: Purdue University extension.

daffodil.about: Yellow and white daffodils flower from late winter to mid spring. In sun or light shade, they come back for many years and slowly spread into clumps. The one thing to remember: let the leaves die back on their own after flowering, because they feed next year's flowers.
daffodil.water: Normal watering is enough for daffodils. Bulbs in the ground rarely need any, only in long dry spells while they are growing. Pots dry out fast, so water them until the leaves die down.
daffodil.feed: They need little food. In the ground they need no feeding at all. In pots, give a high-potassium liquid feed, such as tomato feed, from when the shoots appear until the leaves start to die down.
daffodil.harvest: Snap off faded flowers so the energy goes back into the bulb. Leave the leaves until they turn yellow, about six weeks after flowering. Don't cut, tie or knot them. For the vase, cut daffodils when the bud is about to open.
daffodil.keeps: Cut daffodils ooze a sap that makes other flowers die sooner. Stand them in water on their own overnight before you mix them with others. Don't cut the stems again after that.

problems.name: No flowers (blind daffodils)
problems.fix: You get plenty of leaves but no flowers, from crowded clumps, bulbs planted too shallow or leaves cut off too early. Once the leaves have died back, dig up crowded clumps and pull them apart. Replant the bulbs deeper.

problems.name: Bulb fly
problems.fix: Thin, grassy leaves come up but no flowers and the bulb is soft with a fat grub inside. Throw away soft bulbs. As the leaves die back, firm the soil over the holes so the fly can't reach the bulbs.

problems.name: Rotting bulbs
problems.fix: Bulbs go soft and rot from the bottom, in wet soil or in storage. Plant only firm bulbs, in soil that drains well. Throw away any that feel soft.

daffodil.source: Daffodil care: RHS. pH: University of Connecticut soil testing lab. Pot size: Purdue University extension.

crocus.about: Crocuses grow from corms (like small bulbs) and flower in late winter and early spring. They are among the first food of the year for bees. They come back every year and spread into wide patches in borders and short grass. Let the leaves die back after flowering. In a lawn, don't mow until they have.
crocus.water: Crocuses cope with dry spells and in the ground rarely need water. In a pot, keep the compost moist a few centimetres down while the leaves are up.
crocus.feed: They need little food and none at all in the ground. In a pot, give a high-potassium liquid feed while the leaves are up. It helps next year's flowers.
crocus.harvest: There's no need to snip off the faded flowers. Leave the leaves until they die back. In a lawn, wait to mow until then, so the corms can build up and spread. Once the leaves have died, you can dig up crocuses in pots. Keep them in paper bags somewhere cool and dry until autumn.

problems.name: Squirrels and mice
problems.fix: They dig up and eat the corms after planting. Cover new plantings with chicken wire or metal mesh until the shoots are up.

problems.name: Birds pecking flowers
problems.fix: Sparrows peck the flowers (often the yellow ones) and leave them torn and shredded. Black thread or netting over the clump protects them while they flower.

problems.name: Few flowers
problems.fix: You get fewer flowers each year. Often the leaves were mown or cut before they died back, or the spot has become too shady. Leave the leaves alone and move clumps to a sunnier spot once they have died down for the year.

crocus.source: Crocus care: RHS. pH: University of Connecticut soil testing lab. Pot size: Purdue University extension.

sunflower.about: Sunflowers give you big summer flowers, plus seed for you or the birds. Tall kinds need a strong cane or a wall to be tied to. Dwarf kinds stay short and do well in pots. Protect the seedlings from slugs until they are sturdy.
sunflower.water: They need normal watering. In dry spells, water well at the base of the stem. Tall kinds must not dry out. Plants in pots need water more often, every day in hot weather.
sunflower.feed: Average feeding is right. Dig compost into the bed before sowing. Once flower buds form, give a liquid feed rich in potassium, such as tomato feed, every two weeks. It gives you bigger flowers.
sunflower.harvest: For the vase, cut them in the morning as the petals start to open. For seed, leave the head on until its back turns brown. Cover it with a paper bag or a net to keep the birds off. Then cut it and dry it indoors.
sunflower.keeps: A cut stem lasts about a week in a vase. Change the water every couple of days. Dry seed keeps for months somewhere cool, dry and dark.

problems.name: Slugs and snails
problems.fix: Young plants get eaten down to the stem overnight. Put a collar round each seedling, or start them in pots and plant them out once they are sturdy.

problems.name: Birds
problems.fix: Birds dig up the seed after sowing or pick the ripening heads clean. Cover new sowings with netting. Put a bag over the heads you want to keep.

problems.name: Falling over
problems.fix: Tall stems lean or snap in wind or after rain. Tie them to a strong cane early on, or grow them against a wall or fence.

sunflower.source: Sunflower care: RHS. pH: University of Minnesota extension.

marigold.about: French and African marigolds flower bright orange and yellow from early summer until the first frost. They suit beds, pots and the gaps between vegetables. They are easy to grow, but slugs love the young plants. Pick off the faded flowers and new ones keep coming.
marigold.water: Normal watering is enough. Water in dry spells, at the foot of the plant rather than over the flowers. Pots dry out fast in summer, so check them every day.
marigold.feed: Marigolds need little feeding. Ordinary garden soil is enough. Rich soil or too much feed gives you leaves instead of flowers. In pots, a liquid feed every few weeks keeps them flowering.
marigold.harvest: Every few days, pinch off the faded flowers just below the head. For the vase, cut them when the flowers are fully open.
marigold.keeps: Cut flowers last about a week in a vase. Strip off any leaves that would sit in the water.

problems.name: Slugs and snails
problems.fix: You find holes in the leaves and seedlings gone overnight. Plant out sturdy young plants, not tiny ones. In wet weather, protect them at night.

problems.name: Grey mould
problems.fix: Grey fuzz appears on flowers and stems in cool, wet weather. Take off the rotting flowers. Leave space between plants so they dry quickly.

problems.name: Red spider mite
problems.fix: In hot, dry weather the leaves go pale and speckled, with fine webbing, mostly in greenhouses and pots. Keep plants watered. Mist or hose the undersides of the leaves.

marigold.source: Marigold care: RHS. pH: University of Connecticut soil testing lab.

calendula.about: From early summer into autumn, calendula gives you orange and yellow flowers. It lives for one year but copes with cold. The petals are edible and add colour to salads and rice. It grows in almost any soil and drops seed that comes up all around. Sown in autumn, it survives the winter and flowers early the next year.
calendula.water: Once it's growing well, calendula copes with dry spells. Water seedlings and plants in pots. Keep water off the leaves to slow down powdery mildew.
calendula.feed: It needs little food. Rich soil or a lot of feeding gives soft leaves and fewer flowers. Plants in pots can have a liquid feed once a month.
calendula.harvest: In the morning, cut fully open flowers for the vase or for their petals. Snip off the faded ones every few days. Otherwise the plants set seed and stop flowering.
calendula.keeps: Cut flowers last about a week in a vase. Dry the petals on paper in a warm, airy place and they keep for months in a jar.

problems.name: Powdery mildew
problems.fix: From midsummer a white, dusty coat covers the leaves, worst in dry soil. Water in dry spells, give plants space and pull out badly affected ones. Late sowings stay cleaner.

problems.name: Blackfly
problems.fix: Small black insects cluster on the shoot tips and buds. Rub them off or spray them off with water. Ladybirds and other predators soon follow.

problems.name: Slugs and snails
problems.fix: In wet weather they eat seedlings overnight. Protect young plants at night until they are well grown.

calendula.source: Calendula care: RHS. pH: Utah State University extension.

nasturtium.about: Nasturtiums trail along the ground or climb. You can eat both the bright flowers and the peppery leaves. They do best in poor soil that drains well. Rich soil gives you a mass of leaves and few flowers. They're easy to grow from seed, even for children.
nasturtium.water: Once they're growing in the ground, they cope with dry spells. Water seedlings and plants in pots. If the soil stays very dry for a long time, the flowering stops.
nasturtium.feed: Nasturtiums need very little, so don't feed them at all. Feeding gives you leaves instead of flowers. Grow them in ordinary or poor soil, without compost or manure.
nasturtium.harvest: Pick young leaves and open flowers in the morning, as you need them. Pick the green seeds before they harden and you can pickle them like capers. Picking off faded flowers keeps new ones coming.
nasturtium.keeps: Leaves and flowers wilt quickly. Keep them in a bag in the fridge and use them within a day or two.

problems.name: Blackfly
problems.fix: Thick clusters of black insects sit under the leaves and on the shoot tips. Pick off the worst shoots or hose them down. Ladybirds and hoverflies soon move in.

problems.name: Cabbage white caterpillars
problems.fix: Green caterpillars strip the leaves in late summer. They're the same ones that eat cabbages. Check under the leaves and pick them off by hand.

problems.name: All leaves, few flowers
problems.fix: Big, lush leaves hide just a few flowers, because of rich soil or feeding. Stop feeding. Next year, sow them in a poorer, sunny spot.

nasturtium.source: Nasturtium care: RHS and University of Maryland extension.

zinnia.about: These cut flowers come in bold colours from midsummer to the first frost. The more you cut, the more they flower. Zinnias love heat and sun and they struggle in cold, wet weather. They don't like their roots being disturbed, so sow them where they will flower or in small pots.
zinnia.water: Zinnias need normal watering. In dry spells, water deeply at the base of the plant, because wet leaves bring mildew. Check plants in pots every day in summer.
zinnia.feed: They need little food. Ordinary soil with some compost is enough and too much feed gives soft growth. In pots, give a liquid feed every two weeks once flowering starts.
zinnia.harvest: Cut a flower when it's fully open and the stem is stiff just below the head. A simple test: shake it and the stem shouldn't bend. Cut low down, just above a pair of leaves. Snip off the faded flowers on the rest so new buds keep coming.
zinnia.keeps: Cut zinnias last about a week in a vase. Give them fresh water every couple of days.

problems.name: Powdery mildew
problems.fix: A white, dusty coat appears on the leaves in late summer. Water the soil rather than the leaves, leave space for air and remove the worst leaves. Varieties that resist mildew help too.

problems.name: Leaf spots
problems.fix: In wet weather, brown or dark spots with a pale edge appear on the leaves. Remove spotted leaves and water at the base. Clear the plants away at the end of the season.

problems.name: Slugs and snails
problems.fix: They eat seedlings overnight. Protect them at night or raise them in small pots, then plant them out once they're sturdy.

zinnia.source: Zinnia care: RHS. pH: University of Florida IFAS extension.

cosmos.about: This tall, airy plant lives for one season. It has feathery leaves and daisy-like flowers from midsummer to the first frost and they're good for cutting. It flowers best in poor to average soil. Rich soil gives tall, leafy plants with few flowers. Dwarf types suit pots.
cosmos.water: Once it's settled, cosmos copes with dry spells. Water seedlings, new plants and pots. Too much water, like too much feed, gives you more leaves than flowers.
cosmos.feed: Cosmos needs very little. Don't feed it in the ground. Plants in pots can have a high-potassium liquid feed, such as tomato feed, once a month.
cosmos.harvest: For the vase, cut stems when the buds are just opening, back to a side shoot. Pick off faded flowers every few days, or the plant sets seed and stops flowering.
cosmos.keeps: Cut flowers last from a few days to a week in a vase. Cut them in the cool of the morning.

problems.name: Slugs and snails
problems.fix: They eat seedlings and young plants overnight. Only plant out sturdy plants and protect them at night until they are well grown.

problems.name: All leaves, few flowers
problems.fix: The plants grow tall and lush but flower late and sparsely, because of rich soil, feeding or shade. Stop feeding and keep picking off faded flowers. Next year, choose a sunnier spot with poorer soil.

problems.name: Falling over
problems.fix: Tall plants flop over in wind and rain. Pinch out the tip at about 30 cm so the plants grow bushier. Support them with canes or twiggy sticks.

cosmos.source: Cosmos care: RHS. pH: University of Connecticut soil testing lab.

sweet_pea.about: Sweet peas climb and give scented flowers to cut from early summer. Give them canes, netting or a fence to climb. Pinch out the tip when they are about 10 cm tall and the plants grow bushier. The one rule: keep picking, because once seed pods form they stop flowering. The pods look like garden peas, but they are poisonous.
sweet_pea.water: They need a lot of water. Keep the soil moist all season and water well in dry spells. Dry roots cut the flowering short. In warm weather, pots need water every day.
sweet_pea.feed: Average feeding is right for sweet peas. Before sowing or planting, dig in plenty of compost or well-rotted manure. Once they are growing, a liquid feed every week or two keeps the flowers coming.
sweet_pea.harvest: Every few days, cut stems in the morning when the lowest flowers on them are open. Take off any seed pods you find, or the plant stops flowering.
sweet_pea.keeps: Cut stems last a few days in a vase. The more you cut, the more new flowers come.

problems.name: Aphids
problems.fix: Green insects on the shoot tips and buds can spread viruses that streak and twist the plant. Squash them or hose them off early. Pull out any plants with streaked, stunted growth.

problems.name: Powdery mildew
problems.fix: Late in summer the leaves get a white, dusty coat, worse in dry soil and in crowded spots with still air. Water in dry spells and keep the air moving. Cut out the affected growth.

problems.name: Buds falling off
problems.fix: After cold nights or when the roots are dry, the flower buds turn yellow and fall before they open. Keep the soil moist. It usually stops once the weather settles.

sweet_pea.source: Sweet pea care: RHS. pH: University of Missouri extension. Powdery mildew: Oregon State University extension.

lavender.about: Lavender is a small shrub that stays green all year. Bees love its scented summer flowers, which also dry well. It needs full sun and poor soil that drains quickly. Chalky soil suits it. The one thing to remember: trim it every year after flowering, or it gets straggly and woody.
lavender.water: Once settled, lavender copes well with dry spells. Water new plants regularly in their first summer. After that, plants in the ground rarely need water. A pot dries out fast and needs regular watering in summer.
lavender.feed: It needs very little. Lavender likes soil low in nutrients, so don't feed it. Fertiliser gives soft, floppy growth.
lavender.harvest: For drying, cut stems on a dry morning when the first flowers on the spike open. In late summer, after flowering, cut off the old flower stalks with about 2.5 cm of leafy growth. Never cut into bare wood.
lavender.keeps: Hang small bunches upside down in a dark, airy place until they're dry. In a closed jar, the dried flowers keep their scent for months.

problems.name: Root rot
problems.fix: In wet, heavy soil the plants turn grey and die back, often in winter. Plant on a mound or in a raised bed and add grit to pots. Never leave a pot standing in water.

problems.name: Straggly, woody plant
problems.fix: The stems go bare and woody, with flowers only at the tips. Trim every year after flowering. An old plant that has gone bare won't grow back from old wood, so it's best to replace it.

problems.name: Rosemary beetle
problems.fix: From late summer to spring, small beetles with metallic green and purple stripes eat the leaves and flowers. Their grey grubs do too. Pick them off by hand or shake the plant over a sheet of paper.

lavender.source: Lavender care: RHS. pH: University of California IPM and UMass extension.

field_beans.about: Field beans are a winter green manure, a crop you grow to dig back into the soil. Sown in autumn, they cover bare ground through winter. Their roots open up heavy soil and like all beans they add nitrogen. Dig them in during spring, before the next crop.
field_beans.water: Field beans need very little water. Autumn and winter rain is enough, so only water if the soil is dry when you sow.
field_beans.feed: They need no feeding at all. They make their own nitrogen and it stays in the soil for the next crop.
field_beans.harvest: In spring, any time up to flowering, cut the plants down. Chop them up and let them wilt, then dig them into the top 25 cm of soil. Wait about a month before you sow or plant anything in that bed.

problems.name: Blackfly
problems.fix: In spring, thick clusters of black aphids sit on the shoot tips. Usually you can leave them, as the plants will be dug in soon. If they spread, cut the plants down a little earlier.

problems.name: Slugs and snails
problems.fix: They shelter in the thick cover and then move on to the next crop. After digging in, protect young plants and check for slugs on damp evenings.

field_beans.source: Green manure care: RHS. pH: Oregon State University extension.

winter_rye.about: Winter rye is the hardiest green manure, a crop you grow to dig back into the soil. Sown from late summer to autumn, it keeps growing through winter. It holds the soil and smothers weeds. Its thick roots improve the soil too. Dig it in when spring comes.
winter_rye.water: Rye needs little water and rain is enough. Water only to get the seed going in a dry autumn.
winter_rye.feed: It needs no feeding. Rye grows even on poor, sandy or acid soil. It also takes up nitrogen that winter rain would otherwise wash away.
winter_rye.harvest: In spring, cut it down while it is still short and soft. Chop it, let it wilt and then dig it into the top 25 cm of soil. Older rye is tough and grows back. It holds back the next crop.

problems.name: Small seeds won't come up
problems.fix: While rye rots, it stops small seeds such as carrots and onions from coming up. Wait about a month after digging in before you sow. Or put in young plants or large seeds such as beans instead.

problems.name: Cut too late
problems.fix: Left too long, rye grows tall and tough. It grows back after cutting and can seed itself. Cut it before it reaches about 30 cm.

winter_rye.source: Rye care: RHS and SARE. pH: University of Vermont extension.

crimson_clover.about: Crimson clover is a green manure, a crop you grow for the soil. It adds nitrogen and covers the ground with leaves and red flowers that bees visit. Sow it from spring to late summer. Sown about six to eight weeks before the first frost, it lives through winter and grows on in spring.
crimson_clover.water: It needs little water. Keep the seedbed moist until the seedlings are up. After that, rain is usually enough.
crimson_clover.feed: It needs no feeding. The clover makes its own nitrogen and leaves it in the soil.
crimson_clover.harvest: Cut it down when it flowers, before it sets seed. Once cut to the ground, it doesn't grow back. Dig it into the top 25 cm of soil or leave it on the surface to rot. Then wait about a month before sowing.

problems.name: Clover seeding itself
problems.fix: If you let it set seed, it comes back as a weed among your next crops. Cut it while it's flowering.

problems.name: Slugs and snails
problems.fix: They hide in the thick leaves and then move on to the next crop. After cutting, protect young plants and look for slugs on damp evenings.

crimson_clover.source: Crimson clover care: RHS and SARE. pH: University of California SAREP.

phacelia.about: This fast green manure has feathery leaves and blue flowers that bees love. You grow it for the soil and dig it in later. It covers bare soil, holds on to leftover nutrients and adds organic matter when dug in. It isn't related to any of the usual vegetables, so it fits anywhere when you rotate crops.
phacelia.water: Phacelia needs little water and rain is usually enough. Only water to get a sowing going in dry soil.
phacelia.feed: It needs no feeding. It takes up the nutrients left in the soil and gives them back when you dig it in.
phacelia.harvest: Cut it down when it starts to flower. If you're leaving it for the bees, cut just after, but always before it sets seed. Chop it up and leave it to wilt for a few days. Then dig it into the top of the soil and wait two to three weeks before sowing. An autumn sowing can stay over winter and be dug in when spring comes.

problems.name: Seedlings everywhere
problems.fix: Seedlings come up all over the bed when plants are left to seed. Cut it down before the flowers fade. Pull or hoe the seedlings while they're small.

problems.name: Itchy skin
problems.fix: The bristly stems and leaves can make some people's skin itch or go red. Wear gloves and long sleeves when you cut it and dig it in.

phacelia.source: Phacelia as green manure: RHS. pH: USDA NRCS and British Columbia Ministry of Agriculture.

white_mustard.about: On bare ground, white mustard covers the soil in a few weeks. It's a fast green manure, a crop you grow and then dig into the soil. It smothers weeds and adds organic matter when you dig it in. Sow it from spring to late summer in gaps between crops. It belongs to the cabbage family, so don't grow it where clubroot, a root disease of cabbages, is a problem. When you rotate crops between beds, count it as a cabbage.
white_mustard.water: It needs little water and rain is usually enough. Water the seedbed only in a dry spell, so the seed comes up evenly.
white_mustard.feed: Mustard needs no feeding at all. It takes up the nutrients left in the soil and gives them back when you dig it in.
white_mustard.harvest: Cut it down before it flowers, usually four to eight weeks after sowing. Chop the stems and let them wilt for a few days. Then dig them into the top layer of soil. Wait two to three weeks before sowing or planting there.

problems.name: Clubroot
problems.fix: Because it's related to cabbages, it can carry clubroot and keep the disease in the soil. Don't sow it where clubroot has appeared. Don't sow it just before cabbages, turnips or radishes either.

problems.name: Going to seed
problems.fix: In warm weather it flowers within weeks and the seed comes up as weeds. Check it often in summer and cut it down at the first flowers.
